title: Playwright: Modern End-to-End Test Automation
description: Master Microsoft Playwright for fast, reliable, cross-browser end-to-end testing — from your first test to full CI/CD pipelines, visual regression, and API testing.

lessons.title: Why Playwright? The Modern Automation Landscape
lessons.description: Understand what sets Playwright apart from Selenium and Cypress in 2026.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Why Playwright?

Playwright is Microsoft's open-source automation library for testing modern web apps across **Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox** with a single API. It was built to fix the pain points that plagued Selenium: flaky waits, slow setup, and inconsistent cross-browser behavior.

### Key advantages
- **Auto-waiting**: Playwright waits for elements to be actionable before interacting — no more manual `sleep()` calls.
- **True cross-browser**: One API drives real Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox engines, not just Chrome-based browsers.
- **Built-in parallelism**: Tests run in isolated browser contexts, making parallel execution fast and safe by default.
- **Rich tooling**: Trace Viewer, Codegen, and the Playwright Inspector make debugging failures dramatically faster than older tools.
- **Network-level control**: Native request interception and mocking without a proxy.

By the end of this course, you'll be able to design, write, debug, and scale a production-grade Playwright test suite integrated into a real CI/CD pipeline.

quiz_data.question: What is the primary advantage of Playwright's auto-waiting mechanism?
options: It automatically writes your test assertions for you
It waits for elements to become actionable before performing actions, reducing flaky failures
It slows down tests to match human typing speed
It disables JavaScript before every test
quiz_data.explanation: Auto-waiting means Playwright retries actionability checks (visible, stable, enabled, receives events) before clicking, typing, etc., eliminating most manual waits and flaky failures.

lessons.title: Installing Playwright & Project Setup
lessons.description: Scaffold a real Playwright + TypeScript project from scratch.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Setting Up Your Project

Playwright ships its own scaffolding tool that installs the test runner, browsers, and a starter config in one command.

```bash
npm init playwright@latest
```

This will ask you:
1. TypeScript or JavaScript (**choose TypeScript** — it's the industry standard for serious suites)
2. Where to put tests (default: `tests/`)
3. Whether to add a GitHub Actions workflow (say yes — we'll use it later)
4. Whether to install browsers now (say yes)

### Project structure
```
playwright.config.ts   # global config: browsers, baseURL, retries, reporters
tests/
  example.spec.ts
tests-examples/
```

`playwright.config.ts` is the control center for your entire suite — timeouts, projects (browser/device matrix), and reporters all live here.

lessons.title: Understanding Auto-Waiting & Actionability
lessons.description: Learn exactly what Playwright checks before every action — critical for debugging flaky tests.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Actionability Checks

Before Playwright performs an action like `click()`, it runs a series of **actionability checks** on the element:

- **Attached**: element is in the DOM
- **Visible**: has non-empty bounding box, no `visibility: hidden`
- **Stable**: not animating/transitioning
- **Receives Events**: not obscured by another element
- **Enabled**: not `disabled`

Playwright retries these checks for the duration of the action timeout (default 30s) before failing. This is why Playwright tests are dramatically less flaky than Selenium tests relying on manual `WebDriverWait`.

> **Common mistake**: adding `page.waitForTimeout(2000)` everywhere. This masks real timing issues and slows your suite down for no benefit — trust the auto-waiting instead, and use explicit waits (`waitForResponse`, `waitForLoadState`) only for genuinely async, non-UI-driven state changes.

quiz_data.question: Why should you avoid `page.waitForTimeout()` in most Playwright tests?
options: It is deprecated and throws an error
It only works in Chromium
It masks real timing issues with an arbitrary delay instead of waiting for a real condition
It cannot be used inside a test() block
quiz_data.explanation: Fixed timeouts are either too short (flaky) or too long (slow). Waiting on a real signal — a locator becoming visible, a network response — is always more reliable.

lessons.title: Locator Strategies: Role, Text, and Test IDs
lessons.description: Learn Playwright's recommended, resilient locator hierarchy.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Choosing the Right Locator

Playwright's official recommendation, in priority order:

1. **`getByRole()`** — mirrors how assistive tech and users perceive the page (`button`, `link`, `heading`, etc.)
2. **`getByLabel()` / `getByPlaceholder()`** — for form fields
3. **`getByText()`** — for non-interactive content
4. **`getByTestId()`** — a stable escape hatch (`data-testid` attribute) for elements with no good semantic role

Avoid brittle CSS/XPath selectors tied to implementation details (class names, DOM nesting) — they break the moment a developer restyles the page, even though the user-facing behavior hasn't changed.

```ts
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign up' }).click();
await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('test@example.com');
await page.getByTestId('cart-total').textContent();
```

lessons.title: Handling iframes and Shadow DOM
lessons.description: Automate content that lives inside frames or web components.

quiz_data.question: How does Playwright handle elements inside an open Shadow DOM by default?
options: It cannot access them at all
It requires a special shadowRoot() call before every locator
Standard locators automatically pierce open shadow roots
It only works if you disable Shadow DOM in the browser
quiz_data.explanation: Playwright's engine automatically traverses open shadow roots, so getByRole/getByText/CSS locators 'just work' without extra APIs — unlike Selenium, which requires manual shadowRoot traversal.

lessons.title: Web-First Assertions
lessons.description: Write assertions that retry automatically until they pass or time out.

quiz_data.question: What is the key benefit of `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` over `expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true)`?
options: It is shorter to type
It automatically retries until the condition is true or the timeout elapses
It works only in headless mode
It disables auto-waiting for that one call
quiz_data.explanation: Web-first assertions poll the condition repeatedly within the timeout window, matching how real UIs update asynchronously — a single isVisible() check has no such retry.

quiz_data.question: What is the main benefit of using page.route() to mock the /api/payments endpoint with an aborted request?
options: It speeds up the real payment gateway
It lets you test how the UI handles a failed network request without needing a real failure to occur
It permanently disables the payments API
It is required before every test regardless of what you're testing
quiz_data.explanation: Mocking lets you deterministically simulate failure/edge-case scenarios (timeouts, 500s, malformed payloads) that would be difficult or flaky to trigger against a real backend.

lessons.title: Visual Regression Testing
lessons.description: Catch unintended UI changes with screenshot comparison.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Screenshot Assertions

```ts
await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('dashboard.png');
await expect(page.getByTestId('pricing-card')).toHaveScreenshot('pricing-card.png');
```

On first run, Playwright generates baseline images. On subsequent runs, it pixel-diffs against the baseline and fails if the difference exceeds a configurable threshold (`maxDiffPixelRatio`).

### Best practices
- Mask dynamic content (timestamps, avatars) with the `mask` option to avoid false positives
- Run visual tests in CI against a consistent OS/browser version — screenshots differ subtly across platforms
- Update baselines deliberately (`--update-snapshots`), never blindly in CI

lessons.title: Trace Viewer & Debugging Failures
lessons.description: Use Playwright's most powerful debugging tool to diagnose CI failures.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Trace Viewer

Enable tracing in config:
```ts
use: { trace: 'on-first-retry' }
```

When a test fails (and is retried), Playwright records a full trace: DOM snapshots at every step, network requests, console logs, and screenshots. Open it with:
```bash
npx playwright show-trace trace.zip
```

You get a timeline you can scrub through, seeing the exact DOM state at the moment of failure — this eliminates the classic 'works on my machine, fails in CI' debugging nightmare, since you can inspect exactly what the CI browser saw.

Other debugging tools:
- `npx playwright test --debug` — step through with the Playwright Inspector
- `npx playwright codegen` — record actions and generate locators automatically
- `await page.pause()` — drop into the inspector mid-test

lessons.title: Parallelization & Sharding
lessons.description: Scale your suite across workers and CI machines.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Two Levels of Parallelism

1. **Workers** — Playwright runs test *files* in parallel processes on one machine (`workers: 4` in config, or `--workers=4`)
2. **Sharding** — split the entire suite across multiple CI machines

```bash
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
# ...run these 4 shards on 4 parallel CI jobs
```

### Test isolation is what makes this safe
Each test gets a brand-new browser context (cookies, storage, cache all isolated) by default, so tests can run in any order, in any worker, without leaking state — a huge structural advantage over frameworks where shared browser sessions cause order-dependent flakiness.

lessons.title: CI/CD Integration with GitHub Actions
lessons.description: Wire your Playwright suite into a real automated pipeline.
lessons.content_markdown:
## A Production-Ready Workflow

```yaml
name: E2E Tests
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: playwright-report-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: playwright-report/
```

Key points: `--with-deps` installs OS-level browser dependencies in the CI image; uploading the report as an artifact (even `if: always()` on failure) means every PR has a downloadable, inspectable report and traces.

quiz_data.question: Why should you upload the Playwright report as a CI artifact even when the job fails?
options: It is required for the workflow to be valid YAML
So you can inspect traces and screenshots of the failure without re-running the suite locally
It automatically fixes failing tests
GitHub Actions deletes logs immediately otherwise
quiz_data.explanation: Uploading the HTML report/traces as an artifact preserves full failure context (DOM state, network, screenshots) so you can debug a CI-only failure without needing to reproduce it locally.

lessons.title: Capstone Knowledge Check
lessons.description: Final assessment covering the full course.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Final Review

Before moving on, make sure you can confidently answer:

- Why is `getByRole()` preferred over CSS selectors?
- What's the difference between a web-first assertion and a generic one?
- How do fixtures reduce duplication compared to `beforeEach`?
- When would you mock a network response vs. hit the real backend?
- What does `storageState` buy you across a large suite?

If any of these feel shaky, revisit the relevant module before starting your own project — these five ideas are the backbone of every well-architected Playwright suite.

quiz_data.question: In a well-architected Playwright suite, what is `storageState` primarily used for?
options: Storing test result history
Persisting and reusing an authenticated browser session across tests to skip repeated logins
Saving screenshots for visual regression
Configuring which browsers to run
quiz_data.explanation: storageState captures cookies and localStorage after a one-time login, letting every subsequent test start pre-authenticated — a major speed and reliability win.
